title: Low temperature magnetic structure and lattice response in SmCuAs$_2$
authors: M. G. Kim, C. Neupane, Y. Yu, R. Acevedo-Esteves, C. Nelson, D. Evans, E. D. Mun, D. F. Agterberg, J. -W. Kim
abstract: We investigated the structural and magnetic properties of single-crystalline SmCuAs$_2$ using high-resolution synchrotron X-ray diffraction and X-ray resonant magnetic scattering (XRMS) at the Sm $L_2$ and $L_3$ edges. Temperature-dependent diffraction measurements confirm that SmCuAs$_2$ maintains its tetragonal symmetry from room temperature down to 8 K, with lattice parameters showing anomalous behavior below the resistivity minimum ($T \approx$ 30 K). Notably, the \textbf{c}-axis lattice parameter exhibits a plateau and subsequent increase near the Néel temperature, indicating magnetoelastic coupling. XRMS measurements reveal a commensurate antiferromagnetic structure with a propagation vector \textbf{\textit{q}} = (0, 0, 0.5). Our measurement shows that the Sm moments are aligned within the \textbf{\textit{ab}} plane and arranged in a $++--$ stacking along the \textbf{\textit{c}}-axis. Comparison with related \textit{RE}CuAs$_2$ compounds (\textit{RE} = Pr, Nd, and Gd) suggests that in-plane moment orientation and associated magnetic frustration play a key role in the emergence of the resistivity minimum. Differences in spin-orbit and magnetoelastic coupling across the series highlight their importance in governing low-temperature transport behavior.
summary: This paper experimentally characterizes the structure and magnetism of SmCuAs2 using synchrotron X-ray techniques. It reveals an antiferromagnetic state with moments confined to the ab-plane, while anomalous lattice parameter changes near magnetic transitions confirm significant magnetoelastic coupling. The findings highlight how moment orientation and magnetic frustration govern low-temperature transport properties in this class of materials.
main_problem: The study investigates the structural and magnetic properties of SmCuAs2, focusing on the interplay between lattice response, magnetism, and a resistivity minimum observed at low temperatures.
main_result: The compound exhibits an in-plane antiferromagnetic structure with a specific stacking pattern along the c-axis, and anomalous lattice parameter behavior suggests strong magnetoelastic coupling near magnetic transitions.
method: The research employed high-resolution synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) for structural measurements and X-ray Resonant Magnetic Scattering (XRMS) to determine the precise magnetic ordering vector and moment orientation.
model_or_system: The physical system is single-crystalline SmCuAs2, which belongs to a family of RECuAs2 compounds known for complex low-temperature electronic behavior, including resistivity minima preceding antiferromagnetic ordering.
key_observables: Lattice parameters (a and c), magnetic Bragg peak positions ($\mathbf{q} = (0, 0, 0.5)$), and temperature dependence of these observables relative to the resistivity minimum ($T \approx 30$ K) and Néel temperature ($T_N$).
important_parameters: Temperature range down to 8 K; magnetic propagation vector $\mathbf{q} = (0, 0, 0.5)$; comparison across the RECuAs2 series.
main_assumptions: The anomalous lattice behavior is attributed to magnetoelastic coupling, and the observed magnetic structure is dictated by in-plane moment alignment ($\mathbf{m} \perp c$).
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows XRD results detailing the plateau/increase in the c-lattice parameter near the resistivity minimum. Figure 2 presents XRMS data confirming the commensurate AFM order and determining the moment orientation via energy scans.
paper_structure: The paper systematically uses temperature-dependent XRD to map lattice changes, followed by detailed XRMS analysis to pinpoint the magnetic structure ($\mathbf{q}$ vector and moment direction), culminating in a comparison with related compounds to establish the role of magnetoelastic coupling.
why_interesting: This work provides experimental evidence linking structural anomalies (lattice parameter changes) directly to magnetic ordering phenomena via magnetoelastic coupling, which is a key area of study in strongly correlated materials physics.
